title: When to name a pattern
summary: A pattern is a force plus a structure; skip the name when a function is enough.

parts.rule: A design pattern is a named answer to a recurring force. In an interview, state the force first, then the name, then the cost in extra types or indirection. When the variation is only one boolean branch, keep a plain conditional. If you cannot name the force, you are decorating code with classes. Patterns are communication tools, not trophies.
parts.why: Junior answers spray pattern names without pain. Senior answers decline a pattern when the force is missing. Interviewers listen for that refusal skill as much as for recognition of the famous name.
parts.example: Force: ranking algorithms will change and the feed renderer should not. Name: strategy. Cost: 1 type per algorithm plus a seam to inject it. Counterexample: a boolean isPremium that picks one of two hard-coded fee formulas — a plain conditional is enough; a Strategy hierarchy is theater. Another force: you must undo user edits — command with an undo stack earns its name. Without undo, a simple function call to applyEdit is enough. Practice: given three one-screen designs, say which one carries a real force and which one is a helper wearing a fancy hat. Say the force before the class name. Say the force before the class name. Say the force before the class name. Say the force before the class name.
parts.use: Reach for a named pattern when two or more variants will appear, when teams need a shared vocabulary, or when the cost of indirection is clearly paid by testability or extension. Lead with the force in speech.
parts.refuse: Refuse a pattern whose force you cannot state in one sentence. Refuse wrapping a single function in three interfaces. Refuse collecting patterns like trading cards. Refuse renaming a plain helper to a famous pattern to sound senior.

body:
Rule. A design pattern is a named answer to a recurring force. In an interview, state the force first, then the name, then the cost in extra types or indirection. When the variation is only one boolean branch, keep a plain conditional. If you cannot name the force, you are decorating code with classes. Patterns are communication tools, not trophies.

Why it matters. Junior answers spray pattern names without pain. Senior answers decline a pattern when the force is missing. Interviewers listen for that refusal skill as much as for recognition of the famous name.

Worked example. Force: ranking algorithms will change and the feed renderer should not. Name: strategy. Cost: 1 type per algorithm plus a seam to inject it. Counterexample: a boolean isPremium that picks one of two hard-coded fee formulas — a plain conditional is enough; a Strategy hierarchy is theater. Another force: you must undo user edits — command with an undo stack earns its name. Without undo, a simple function call to applyEdit is enough. Practice: given three one-screen designs, say which one carries a real force and which one is a helper wearing a fancy hat. Say the force before the class name. Say the force before the class name. Say the force before the class name. Say the force before the class name.

[[diagram:force]]

When to use. Reach for a named pattern when two or more variants will appear, when teams need a shared vocabulary, or when the cost of indirection is clearly paid by testability or extension. Lead with the force in speech.

When to refuse. Refuse a pattern whose force you cannot state in one sentence. Refuse wrapping a single function in three interfaces. Refuse collecting patterns like trading cards. Refuse renaming a plain helper to a famous pattern to sound senior.
